In 2024, the median full-service restaurant kept just 2.8% of sales as pre-tax income, according to the National Restaurant Association (NRA) in its[State of the Restaurant Industry 2026](https://restaurant.org/research-and-media/research/research-reports/state-of-the-industry/) report. At a margin that thin, one overstaffed Tuesday or one over-ordered case of produce can sting.


Restaurant forecasting is how you stop guessing andstart planning . You take your past sales, add what you know is coming, and predict how busy you’ll be, so you can schedule, prep, and order accordingly.


Below you’ll find what to forecast, four forecasting methods, a seven-step process for your spreadsheet, and a few tools worth a look.

## **Restaurant Forecasting in Short: What to Forecast, How, and With What**


Restaurant forecasting predicts your sales, guest counts, and labor needs so you can plan shifts, prep, and orders ahead of time, and you don’t need special tools to get started. Here’s the short version:


- Start small: forecast sales and guest counts by day and daypart.
- Use your history: take last year’s same period and adjust it for recent trends.
- Turn the numbers into a plan: convert sales into labor hours, prep, and orders.
- Check your work: compare your forecast to your actual results every week.
- Add tools when you’re ready: restaurant sales forecasting tools help once you want hourly or item-level forecasts.


## **What Is Restaurant Forecasting?**


Restaurant forecasting predicts sales, guest counts, labor needs, inventory, and costs from past performance plus known upcoming conditions. Owners use it to decide how many people to schedule, how much to prep and order, and how much cash to keep on hand.


Restaurant forecasting breaks into four types: sales and demand, labor, inventory, and cost and cash flow.


### **Sales and Demand Forecasting**


Restaurant sales forecasting estimates your revenue, while restaurant demand forecasting looks at the volume behind it: guests, orders, and menu items. Covers are the guests you serve, and average check is your sales divided by the number of checks.


### **Labor Forecasting**


Restaurant[labor forecasting](https://www.joinhomebase.com/employee-scheduling/labor-forecasting) estimates the hours you need by daypart and role. Your labor cost percentage is labor cost divided by sales, and prime cost is food and beverage cost plus labor, the bulk of the costs you can steer. Our free[restaurant labor cost calculator](https://www.joinhomebase.com/labor-cost-calculator/restaurant) does the labor cost percentage math for you.


### **Inventory Forecasting**


Restaurant inventory forecasting turns expected menu item sales into prep and ingredient quantities, so you can order enough without over-ordering perishables.


### **Cost and Cash-Flow Forecasting**


Cost forecasting predicts what food, payroll, rent, and utilities will run you, and cash-flow forecasting predicts when money comes in and goes out. Together they make restaurant budgeting and forecasting work as a pair.


## **Why Restaurant Forecasting Matters in 2026**


Sales are growing on paper, but margin is the squeeze. According to the NRA’s[State of the Restaurant Industry 2026 executive summary](https://go.restaurant.org/rs/078-ZLA-461/images/SOI-2026-ExecutiveSummary.pdf?version=1) , restaurant and foodservice sales are forecast to reach $1.55 trillion in 2026, but real, inflation-adjusted growth is only 1.3%. Meanwhile, 42% of operators said they weren’t profitable in 2025.


The pressure shows up in a few places:


- Traffic: In the NRA’s 2026 report, more than six in 10 operators said customer traffic fell in 2025.
- Margins: The same report puts median pre-tax income at 2.8% of sales for full-service and 4% for limited-service restaurants.
- Prices: The U.S. Department of Agriculture’s Economic Research Service (ERS) forecasts food-away-from-home prices up 3.5% in 2026, according to its[Food Price Outlook](https://www.ers.usda.gov/data-products/food-price-outlook/summary-findings) .


You can’t control traffic or food prices, but you can control how well your team and your prep match the day ahead.


### **Are Restaurants Struggling in 2026?**


Many are, especially full-service restaurants.[Black Box Intelligence](https://blackboxintelligence.com/blog/what-bbi-data-tells-us-about-unit-closures-in-2026/) flagged 9% of full-service and 4% of limited-service restaurant locations as at risk of closing in 2026, meaning they lost 30% or more of their peak sales in 2025. The encouraging part is that about 85% to 90% of the industry is holding at or near its peak.


## **What Are the Four Restaurant Forecasting Methods?**


The four restaurant sales forecasting methods are qualitative (judgment and research), time series (patterns in past sales), causal (sales linked to drivers like weather or events), and simulation (testing what-if scenarios). A good starting point for a small restaurant is time series plus your own judgment.


What Are the Four Restaurant Forecasting Methods? **Method** **What It Uses** **Best For** **Watch Out For**


Qualitative Your judgment and local knowledge New restaurants with no history Bias


Time series Past sales patterns Steady businesses Sudden spikes


Causal Drivers like weather and events Restaurants with clear sales drivers Guessing at cause and effect


Simulation What-if scenarios Budgets and cash flow Made-up inputs


### **Qualitative Forecasting**


Qualitative forecasting relies on judgment: your read on the neighborhood, what regulars tell you, and the festival coming to town next week. It’s the best starting point for a new restaurant with no history, and the main risk is bias, so write your guess down and check it later.


### **Time Series Forecasting**


Time series forecasting looks for patterns in past sales, like comparing this Friday to the last four Fridays or to the same Friday last year. It works well when your business is steady, though it can miss spikes.


### **Causal Forecasting**


Causal forecasting links your sales to the things that drive them, like weather, events, reservations, and promotions. For the weather impact on restaurant sales forecasting, compare your rainy and sunny days: a rainy Saturday might lift takeout and cut dine-in. Test your own numbers before trusting a rule of thumb; a spreadsheet trendline can serve as your restaurant forecasting model.


### **Simulation (What-If) Forecasting**


Simulation forecasting tests scenarios, like what happens if sales drop 10% next quarter or wages go up. You plug in the numbers and see what happens to your labor percentage and profit.


## **What Are the 7 Steps of Restaurant Forecasting?**


The seven steps are: decide what the forecast is for, choose what to forecast, set a time horizon, pick a method, gather your data, make the forecast, then check it against actual results and put it to work.


Here’s how to do restaurant forecasting, using the standard process from Heizer, Render, and Munson’s Operations Management textbook, applied to forecasting restaurant sales.


### **1. Decide What the Forecast Is For**


Pick one decision to forecast for. A good pick for a small restaurant is next week’s schedule, since it affects your team right away.


### **2. Choose What to Forecast**


Start with sales and covers by daypart, like lunch and dinner, and add average check, labor hours, or menu items once you’re comfortable.


### **3. Set Your Time Horizon**


Match your horizon to the decision: forecast next week for the schedule, tomorrow for prep, and the next few months for cash.


### **4. Pick a Method**


Start with time series, then adjust with your own judgment. Imagine last October’s Friday dinners averaged $4,200, and the last eight weeks ran 6% above the same weeks last year. You’d plan for about $4,450, then adjust for known events.


### **5. Gather Your Data**


Pull sales by daypart from your point-of-sale (POS) system, along with guest counts and the hours from your time clock. Then add reservations, catering orders, local events, weather, and promotions. It’s worth cleaning up the data first, because missing transactions and wrong clock outs can skew your numbers.


### **6. Make the Forecast**


Two simple formulas do most of the work:


- Forecast sales = expected guests × expected average check
- Labor hours = forecast sales ÷ your target sales per labor hour


Here’s a restaurant forecasting example. Imagine you expect 120 dinner guests at a $28 average check, which comes to $3,360. With a target of $70 in sales per labor hour, you’d plan for 48 hours.


### **7. Check It Against Actual Results and Adjust**


After the week, compare your forecast to your actual sales. The formula is:


**Forecast Error Percentage = |Actual − Forecast| ÷ Actual × 100**


So if you forecast $3,360 and sold $3,000, you were off by 12%.


Track over-forecasts and under-forecasts separately, because each one costs you something different. A simple spreadsheet works as a restaurant forecasting template, with one row per day and columns for forecast, actual, and error.


## **Forecasting Sales for a New Restaurant**


With no history, forecasting sales for a new restaurant starts with capacity: multiply seats by table turns by services per day. Imagine a 40-seat café with two turns and two services, which gives you 160 guests at full capacity. If you expect to fill about half, plan around 80, then multiply by your expected average check.


Watch foot traffic near your location and re-forecast monthly as actual sales come in. ## **Restaurant Forecasting Software: What to Look For and Options to Try**


Restaurant sales forecasting software uses your POS sales history, and sometimes weather and local events, to predict sales and recommend staffing or ordering. For small restaurants, a strong fit is restaurant scheduling and forecasting software that connects to your POS and turns the forecast into a schedule.


### **What to Look For in Restaurant Forecasting Software**


Before you compare restaurant demand forecasting software, decide what you need it to do. Here are six things to check:


- POS connection: The forecast is only as good as the sales data feeding it.
- Level of detail: Daily forecasts work to start, and hourly or item-level forecasts help as you grow.
- What it forecasts: Sales, labor, inventory, or all three.
- A path to your schedule: The forecast should turn into shifts without retyping.
- Accuracy tracking: You should be able to compare forecast to actual.
- Pricing: Check per-location costs, contract terms, and whether there’s a free plan.

## **Frequently Asked Questions About Restaurant Forecasting**


### **What Is the 30/30/30 Rule for Restaurants?**


The 30/30/30 rule, also called 30/30/30/10, is a budgeting guideline: about 30% of sales goes to food, 30% to labor, and 30% to overhead, leaving 10% for profit. Real margins run thinner. In 2024, median pre-tax income was 2.8% of sales for full-service and 4% for limited-service restaurants, according to the NRA’s[2026 report](https://restaurant.org/research-and-media/research/research-reports/state-of-the-industry/) .


### **What Is the Difference Between a Forecast and a Budget?**


A forecast estimates what’s likely to happen based on past performance and current conditions, while a budget sets what you plan or want to happen. Compare the two regularly to see where results are drifting from your plan.


### **How Often Should You Update a Restaurant Forecast?**


Review next week’s forecast before you build the schedule, then check it daily against actual sales. Update it whenever reservations, weather, events, or costs change.


### **How Much Sales History Do You Need to Forecast?**


A full year lets you compare the same season, but even a few weeks of sales by daypart helps. With little history, lean on your judgment and capacity math, then update quickly as actual numbers come in.


## **Start With One Forecast, Then Build From There**


You don’t need a perfect model to get started. Begin with next week’s sales and labor hours, compare them to what happened, and adjust from there, adding methods and tools as you outgrow the spreadsheet.
